claims.text: Applying an aluminum oxide surface coating improves the high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed intervention is application of an aluminum oxide surface coating to an untreated refractory high-entropy alloy.
The coating is expected to form a protective aluminum oxide layer.
The aluminum oxide layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion reduces oxidation of the alloy.
Restricting oxygen diffusion reduces degradation of the alloy.
At 1000°C in air for 100 hours, the coated alloy will have an oxidation rate at least 50% lower than the untreated alloy.
The intervention is expected to work over a temperature range of 900–1100°C.
The intervention is expected to work in air or oxygen-rich environments.
Coating effectiveness may depend on the specific composition of the refractory high-entropy alloy.
Coating effectiveness may depend on the coating application method.
The proposed experiment compares coated and uncoated samples in air at 1000°C for 100 hours.
Failure of the coated sample to show a significantly lower oxidation rate than the uncoated sample would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifies at least a 50% oxidation-rate reduction, whereas the falsification rule only requires a statistically significant reduction. A significant reduction smaller than 50% would fail the quantitative prediction but would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
